summary: Cladistics for ages 13–14: group organisms by shared DERIVED characters (synapomorphies) and common ancestry, not by overall resemblance. Learners read and build phylogenetic trees from molecular data (DNA sequence alignment, counting differences), confront convergent evolution as a misleading resemblance, see that classification is an evidence-driven hypothesis that revises with new data (birds nested within dinosaurs; whales near hippos/artiodactyls), and meet horizontal gene transfer webbing the tree, plus the molecular clock with its rate-variation uncertainty.
misconceptions: 'Things that look alike are most closely related' — convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated lineages; shared derived characters/DNA are the evidence.
'Higher/more advanced species evolved FROM the living species next to them on the tree' — tips are all modern; they share common ANCESTORS at the nodes, they don't descend from each other.
'Birds and dinosaurs are separate groups' — birds are a lineage within (theropod) dinosaurs.
'Classification is arbitrary or fixed forever' — it is an evidence-based hypothesis that changes as new (esp. molecular) data emerge.
'Evolution is always a branching tree' — horizontal gene transfer (especially in microbes) makes parts of the tree of life a web.
'The molecular clock is exact' — mutation rates vary across lineages/genes, so molecular dates carry uncertainty.

activities.title: Build and revise a tree from character and DNA data
steps: Start with a small matrix of characters and DNA sequences for several species.
Mark which species share DERIVED characters and count sequence differences between pairs.
Group species by shared derived characters so a cladogram assembles, with common ancestors at the nodes and branch points as shared-ancestry hypotheses.

First build a tree using only overall appearance; then add molecular data and shared-derived-character data and observe which species move (e.g. DNA and mammalian features such as mammary glands move a dolphin placed beside sharks across to the mammals; fossil skeletal shared derived characters such as a wishbone and hollow bones place birds inside the dinosaurs, because no DNA is available from non-avian dinosaurs).
State in your own words why adding evidence changed the grouping.
activities.insight: Classification is a testable hypothesis about shared ancestry that changes as new (especially molecular) evidence arrives; grouping is decided by shared derived characters and DNA, not by appearance.

activities.title: The convergence challenge: when resemblance lies
steps: Examine a look-alike pair that are distantly related, e.g. dolphin vs shark/tuna body shape, and contrast this with homologous forelimbs — bird wing, bat wing, and a human arm (or whale flipper) are the same inherited tetrapod forelimb skeleton, even though flight in a bird and a bat evolved independently.
Decide whether the shared streamlined shape is inherited from a common ancestor or arose independently.
Check the grouping against DNA/molecular distance and name deep inherited (homologous) features the dolphin shares with mammals — mammary glands, three middle-ear bones.
Explain why a convergent trait is evidence AGAINST using it to group species.
activities.insight: Convergent evolution produces similar traits in distantly related lineages under similar pressures; shared derived homologies (characters inherited from a common ancestor), tested with DNA, are what arbitrate grouping.

activities.title: Dating nodes and the tree-becoming-web frontier
steps: Use molecular distance to order nodes in time — more sequence differences roughly means longer since the common ancestor, assuming comparable rates.
Apply a molecular-clock estimate to date a node, and note that estimates carry an uncertainty band because mutation rates vary across lineages and genes.
Add cross-branch links representing horizontal gene transfer (especially in microbes) and describe how they turn a purely branching tree into a partial web.
Explain why classification schemes keep being redrawn without this meaning earlier scientists were simply 'wrong'.
activities.insight: Molecular data can both build and date trees, but dates are hypotheses with uncertainty; horizontal gene transfer means ancestry is not always a clean branching tree.

activities.title: Read a cladogram explicitly before building
steps: On a labelled cladogram, identify which two species share the most recent common ancestor.

Point to a node (branch point) and state what it represents (a hypothesised common ancestor); point to a derived character marked on the branch leading to that node and state what it represents (a shared derived character supporting the group that descends from that node).

Given a sequence table, order several species by molecular distance from a chosen reference species, treating fewer differences as a hypothesis of closer relatedness, assuming roughly comparable rates.
Answer: do the species at the tips descend from one another, or from shared ancestors at the nodes?
activities.insight: Tree literacy — nodes as common ancestors, branching as shared-ancestry hypotheses, tips as modern species sharing ancestors rather than descending from each other.

activities.title: Discussion extension: why do textbooks keep redrawing the tree of life?
steps: Discuss, in the role of a systematist, why classifications keep changing and what counts as good evidence for moving a group.
Argue whether the 'tree of life' is better described as a tree or a web, citing horizontal gene transfer.

Explain how you would check a surprising claim (e.g. that birds belong within dinosaurs) using shared derived characters in fossil skeletons (e.g. wishbone, hollow bones, feathers preserved in some theropod fossils). Note that DNA can test how birds relate to living groups (their closest living relatives are crocodilians), but no DNA is available from non-avian dinosaurs.
activities.insight: Classification is an ongoing, evidence-based scientific debate, not a fixed set of labels.

checkQuestion: A dolphin and a tuna both have sleek, streamlined bodies and fins and live in the sea — a tuna looks far more like a dolphin than a mouse does. So should dolphins be grouped with sharks and tuna (fish) rather than with mice (mammals)? How do scientists actually decide?
checkAnswer: No — grouping should be by shared DERIVED characters inherited from a common ancestor (homologies), not by overall resemblance. The dolphin's streamlined shape is convergent evolution: it arose independently for swimming and was not inherited from a fish ancestor. Dolphins share deep inherited features with mice — mammary glands, three middle-ear bones, and a common ancestor confirmed by DNA — so they group with mammals. Shared derived traits and DNA sequence data, not superficial similarity, decide the grouping, which is why the dolphin belongs with the mouse.
